item.title: Ruby cells
item.description:
A ```ruby block is a Ruby cell (go-notebook v0.3.0 and later). The Ruby is rbgo, a Ruby bytecode VM written in Go, with the go-scikit bindings registered over the same Go libraries a Go cell imports:

Ruby Go library Counterpart
Stats go-statistics/stats scipy.stats
Special go-numerics/special scipy.special
Optimize go-numerics/optimize scipy.optimize
Integrate go-numerics/integrate scipy.integrate
DataFrame go-dataframe/dataframe pandas
Plot go-plot/plot matplotlib.pyplot
NDArray go-ndarray/ndarray (rbgo’s own) numpy.ndarray

Every binding calls the Go function it is named after; the bindings’ README lists every name.

The kernel adds github.com/go-scikit/ruby to the notebook’s work module by itself, and builds the worker with -tags rbgo_core (the Ruby language and its numeric stack, without gems). A notebook needs nothing more than go-notebook.

To try the same Ruby line by line, as irb, without a notebook file, run notebook irb.

A mixed notebook

A Go cell makes the data, a Ruby cell fits it with a go-scikit binding, and a Go cell reads the fit back (the file’s prose is left out here):

```go
xs := []float64{2.1, 3.4, 1.9, 5.6, 4.4, 3.3, 2.8, 4.9}
```

```ruby
fit = Stats::Normal.fit(xs)
loc, scale = fit.loc, fit.scale
ks = Stats.ks_1samp(xs) { |x| fit.cdf(x) }
pvalue = ks.pvalue
fit
```

```go
import "fmt"

fmt.Printf("loc %.4f, scale %.4f, KS p-value %.4f\n", loc, scale, pvalue)
```

In a module whose go.mod has tool github.com/go-notebook/notebook/cmd/notebook and requires github.com/go-notebook/notebook v0.3.0:

$ go tool notebook run first.md
── cell 0 (line 6, ran in 0s)
── cell 1 (line 13, ran in 366µs)
 #<Stats::Normal loc=3.55, scale=1.2359207094308275>
── cell 2 (line 23, ran in 3µs)
 loc 3.5500, scale 1.2359, KS p-value 0.9381

In the Ruby cell xs is an Array of Floats; in the last Go cell loc, scale and pvalue are float64s. (A real transcript, from go-notebook v0.3.0 with go-scikit/ruby v0.1.0; the line numbers are those of the full file.) A larger example, with an NDArray and a plot, is examples/mixed.md.

The rules

Ruby cells follow the rules of Go cells: one definition per name, no assignment to another cell’s variable, and a name starting with _ stays in its cell. The names come from rbgo’s own parser: a cell defines the locals it assigns at its top level, and the methods, constants, classes and modules it defines there; it uses the names it reads before assigning them.

The Ruby cells share one interpreter, so their top-level locals persist from cell to cell. Dependencies, caching and re-runs work across the two languages as for Go alone: a Ruby cell runs again only when it, or a cell it reads, changed.

A cell that ends in an expression shows its value: a Plot figure as SVG, anything else as its inspect (an NDArray in NumPy’s form). An exception fails the cell with file:line: message (Class) at the notebook’s line, followed by the backtrace frames in the notebook (twelve at most).

How values cross between Go and Ruby

Only variables cross. A Go cell sees a Ruby cell’s top-level locals, not its methods, constants or classes, nor a local named like a Go keyword or predeclared identifier (len, type, int). A Ruby cell sees a Go cell’s variables, not its funcs or types.

Go to Ruby. Before a Ruby cell runs, each Go variable it reads becomes a Ruby local of the same name (a constant when the name starts with an upper-case letter):

  • numbers, strings and booleans as such;
  • slices as Arrays, maps as Hashes;
  • an *ndarray.Array as the NDArray itself, not a copy;
  • any other value (a *plot.Figure, a struct) as an object that comes back to Go as itself.

Ruby to Go. After a Ruby cell runs, each local it assigns becomes a Go variable whose type is the type of its value:

Ruby value Go type
nil any (nil)
true, false bool
Integer int64 (*big.Int when it does not fit)
Float float64
String string
Symbol ruby.Symbol
Complex complex128
Rational *big.Rat
NDArray *ndarray.Array, the same array
Array of all Floats, all Integers, all Strings, all booleans []float64, []int64, []string, []bool
any other Array []any
Hash with String keys map[string]any
Hash with Symbol keys map[ruby.Symbol]any
any other Hash map[any]any
a go-scikit object the Go value it wraps: *plot.Figure, stats.TTestResult, *optimize.Result, …
any other Ruby object ruby.Value, which a Go cell can Call

The type comes from the value, so it is known once the Ruby cell has run. A Go cell that reads a Ruby variable whose type is not known yet waits: the Ruby cell runs, then the Go cell is compiled with the type and runs, in the same run. When a later edit changes the type, only the Go cells that read the variable are compiled again.

Limits

A notebook is a program, and it runs with your rights. A Ruby cell can reach what a Go cell can: files through File, IO and Dir, other processes through Process, the environment through ENV, and the bindings that write files (DataFrame#write_csv, Plot::Figure#save_svg). The rbgo_core build leaves out the network libraries (socket, net/*, openssl): requiring one raises LoadError. Run only notebooks you trust.

Every cell runs in the worker, a process of its own, so the kernel survives whatever a cell does:

What the cell does What happens
runs too long with --timeout 30s, its worker is killed and the cell fails with “stopped: the cell ran longer than 30s”; the next run starts a new worker
holds too much memory with --memory 512 (MiB), the garbage collector keeps under the limit as long as it can, then the worker is stopped and the cell fails with “stopped: the cell went over its memory limit”
recurses without end Ruby raises SystemStackError, shown with twelve frames
asks for an impossible allocation ('x' * 2**62) Ruby raises NoMemoryError
calls exit or exit! a SystemExit fails the cell; the worker lives on
kills its own process (Process.kill, not on Windows; os.Exit in Go) the cell says so, and the next run restarts the worker

Both limits apply to Go and Ruby cells alike and are off by default. The memory limit counts the Go heap, sampled every 20 ms; memory held outside it (a large stack, a mapped file) is bounded only by the operating system.

In the browser

The playground runs Ruby cells too, with no server: the same rbgo and go-scikit bindings, compiled to WebAssembly. The page fetches the Ruby core (playground-ruby.wasm) only when the open notebook has a Ruby cell, so a visitor who runs only Go never downloads it. The Ruby there has no bridge to the page’s JavaScript and no file system, and every figure a cell shows goes through an allowlist SVG sanitizer before it reaches the page. Try the Ruby examples on go-notebook’s own playground, go-statistics and go-numerics.

item.title: An interactive session: notebook irb
item.description:
notebook irb (go-notebook v0.5.0 and later) is an interactive Ruby session, as Ruby’s irb, on the Ruby that runs Ruby cells: rbgo with the go-scikit bindings — Stats, Special, Optimize, Integrate, DataFrame, Plot and NDArray. There is no notebook file: inputs are typed, evaluated and shown one at a time.

$ notebook irb
irb(main):001> x = [2.1, 3.4, 1.9, 5.6]
=> [2.1, 3.4, 1.9, 5.6]
irb(main):002> fit = Stats::Normal.fit(x)
=> #<Stats::Normal loc=3.25, scale=1.4739402972983673>
irb(main):003> fit.loc
=> 3.25
irb(main):004> _ * 2
=> 6.5
irb(main):005> def sq(v)
irb(main):006* v * v
irb(main):007* end
=> :sq
irb(main):008> sq(3)
=> 9
irb(main):009> x = x.sum
=> 13.0
irb(main):010> raise "boom"
boom (RuntimeError)
 from (irb):10:in '<main>'
irb(main):011> s = "multi
irb(main):012" line string"
=> "multi\nline string"
irb(main):013> exit

(A real transcript, from notebook irb < session.rb: when standard input is not a terminal, each line is echoed after its prompt.)

The first session builds the worker program, once (building the Ruby worker; it fetches and compiles rbgo the first time); later sessions start at once. It needs the Go toolchain, as notebook run does.

What it does as irb does

Results => and the value’s inspect after each input; _ is the last value
Exceptions message (Class) and the frames in the session (twelve at most); the session goes on, and _ keeps the last value that was not one
Reassignment any local may be assigned again: there is no dependency graph here, unlike in a notebook
Multi-line input an input that is not finished — an open def, do, bracket, string, heredoc, or a line ending in an operator or \ — continues on the next line, under irb’s continuation prompt (*, or the quote of an open string)
Ending exit, quit, exit! or Ctrl-D; Ruby’s exit inside an input ends it too
Ctrl-C abandons the line being typed; during an input, stops it (see below)

Whether an input is finished is decided by rbgo’s own parser (go-ruby-parser): an input it finds ending in the middle of a construct continues. Where the parser accepts an unterminated literal as it is (a string, a heredoc, a regexp, =begin), the port of IRB’s lexer in go-ruby-irb says it is open. Any other syntax error is evaluated, for Ruby to report.

The line editor

On a terminal, lines are edited with go-ruby-reline, a pure-Go port of Ruby’s Reline, through its terminal package — on Linux, macOS and Windows 10 and later:

  • emacs keys (Ctrl-A/E/K/U/W/Y, Alt-F/B, …), the arrow, Home, End and Delete keys, undo;
  • history with Up and Down, and Ctrl-R to search it; a multi-line input comes back whole;
  • bracketed paste: a pasted block is inserted as it is, newlines included;
  • Tab completion of locals, methods of main, keywords, constants and the bindings (St → Stats, Stats::Nor → Stats::Normal), and of the methods of a variable’s value or a constant path’s (x.so → x.sort, Stats::Normal.fi → Stats::Normal.fit), as IRB’s default completor does. A word is completed by asking the worker about the names it holds: completion never evaluates an expression the word contains (xs.first.ti completes to nothing), so pressing Tab runs none of your code. A completion that takes more than five seconds (a methods method that does not return) stops the worker, and the next input says so.

When standard input is not a terminal, lines are read as they come, with no editing, and echoed after their prompt, so notebook irb < script.rb prints a transcript and a session can be scripted and tested.

Limits: each input in a worker

The interpreter runs in a worker process, as a notebook’s cells do, and --timeout and --memory apply to each input:

$ notebook irb --timeout 3s --memory 256
irb(main):001> kept = 1
=> 1
irb(main):002> loop { }
stopped: the input ran longer than 3s, the limit; its worker was killed
notebook irb: the session's state (locals, methods, classes) is lost; the next input starts a new worker
irb(main):003> kept
undefined local variable or method 'kept' for main (NameError)
 from (irb):3:in '<main>'

rbgo cannot be interrupted in the middle of an evaluation, so stopping an input — a limit, or Ctrl-C — kills its worker: the prompt stays, the next input gets a new worker, and the session says that the old one’s locals, methods and classes are gone. The worker is in a process group of its own, so Ctrl-C in the terminal reaches the session, which stops the worker; it is not the worker that dies of it.

The worker’s standard input is empty (gets returns nil): its own is the protocol with the session.

Figures

A value that shows itself — a Plot figure — is never printed as SVG:

irb(main):014> fig, ax = Plot.subplots
=> [#<Plot::Figure 640x480>, #<Plot::Axes>]
irb(main):015> ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [3, 1, 2])
=> nil
irb(main):016> fig
=> #<Plot::Figure 640x480> (a figure: --svg-dir saves it as SVG)

With --svg-dir figures, each figure an input shows is written to figures/figure-N.svg, and the line says where.

Saving the session as a notebook

--save session.md writes, when the session ends, the inputs that ran as ```ruby cells, which notebook run session.md runs again. A notebook has rules a session does not — each name is defined by one cell, and _ stays in its cell — so the inputs are grouped:

  • one cell per input, by default;
  • an input that defines or assigns a name an earlier cell defines (x = x.sum after x = [...], a method defined again) is joined to that cell, with every input in between;
  • an input that reads _ is joined to the one before it, which then assigns _ its value (_ = begin … end), as irb did;
  • should the result still break a rule (two methods that call each other, defined in two inputs), all the inputs make one cell.

The inputs that raised an exception are left out, and the notebook says how many. For the session above:

```ruby
x = [2.1, 3.4, 1.9, 5.6]
fit = Stats::Normal.fit(x)
_ = begin
fit.loc
end
_ * 2
def sq(v)
 v * v
end
sq(3)
x = x.sum
```

```ruby
s = "multi
line string"
```

The saved notebook is a record of what ran, not of the session’s state: a worker stopped in the middle of the session does not change it.

History

The inputs are kept in irb_history under the user config directory’s go-notebook (~/.config/go-notebook/irb_history on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/go-notebook/irb_history on macOS, %AppData%\go-notebook\irb_history on Windows), in irb’s format (a multi-line input’s lines joined by \):

  • the inputs only, never their values;
  • the last --history-size of them (1000, irb’s default; 0 keeps no file);
  • mode 0600 (read and written by its owner only), in a directory made with mode 0700; it is written through a new file renamed over the old one, and another session’s inputs saved meanwhile are kept;
  • a file that cannot be read, or one over 8 MiB, is left alone, and the session keeps no history.

Flags

Flag Default Meaning
-t, --timeout 0 (no limit) stop an input that runs longer than this
-m, --memory 0 (no limit) stop an input whose worker holds more than this many MiB of Go heap
-s, --save write the session, at its end, as a notebook
--svg-dir save each figure as an SVG file in this directory
--history see above the history file
--history-size 1000 how many inputs the history keeps; 0: no history file
-w, --work go-notebook/irb under the user cache directory where the worker is built
--runtime-src use the go-notebook source tree at this path instead of a released runtime

NOTEBOOK_REPLACE points modules of the worker’s module at local checkouts, as for a notebook (see the command).

Not in it

Go cells: a session is Ruby only. irb’s own commands beyond exit and quit (ls, show_source, edit, …), pp and inspect modes, and colour are not there yet.
